Discussed memory fragmentation, KV cache eviction behavior, quantization side-effects, and retry semantics for streaming completions. Agreed on log collection, repro runs on dedicated nodes, and conservative retry/timeouts for non-idempotent streaming requests.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 min
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Chu (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SRE), Jon Park (Redwood Support), Sara Kim (Aegis SRE), Tom Becker (Aegis ML Infra), Priya Nair (Aegis CTO), Carlos Ruiz (Aegis Backend)

[00:00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for making time. quick goal for today's deep dive is to get to root cause on the OOMs and the intermittent cuda timeouts you flagged, and then align on retry/timeouts and next steps.
[00:00:21] Tom: yeah thanks. we've been seeing these during our nightly large-batch streaming runs, roughly 128 concurrent streams, a lot of long sequences, so sometimes p95 seq around 1k tokens. we see OOMs on the nodes and occasional driver timeouts. it's blocking our pilot.
[00:00:38] Ethan: okay, can you confirm whether these are 16-bit float runs or you've tried 8-bit quantized runs as well? sometimes quantization changes memory layout and can actually increase peak working set if not aligned.
[00:00:52] Tom: right now we run fp16 on the dedicated fleet. we tried int8 quant a week ago and actually saw slightly more OOMs - we assumed quant would reduce memory but it seemed to bump something. we may have misconfigured the quant profile.
[00:01:12] Sara: also noticed that the KV cache size spikes right before the OOMs; we think prefix caching + largebatching is causing more live KV memory than expected.
[00:01:24] Lena: that jives. Redwood's runtime keeps a per-request KV cache unless prefix dedupe kicks in - and if you have long contexts without prefix overlap, cache doesn't help. can you share your prompt patterns so we can reason about eviction?
[00:01:40] Carlos: most requests are relatively unique, only about 10% share prefixes. batching is aggressive to keep token cost down.
[00:01:52] Ethan: got it. couple of threads to explore: memory fragmentation on CUDA, pinned host memory pressure, kv cache eviction policy (LRU vs size-based), and how quant bits affect kernel memory alignment. also need to understand the exact cuda errors - is it cudaErrorIllegalAddress, or driver timeout (TDR) or OOM from allocator?

[00:02:20] Tom: logs show something like 'CUDA out of memory' and occasionally 'CUDA timeout detected (context lost)'. we also see the OS killing processes (oom_killer) on some nodes.
[00:02:33] Jon: if the kernel crashes due to TDR, you'll see context lost and then the process dies; that's different than allocator OOM which can be handled with retries.

[00:02:50] Priya: quick Q: for streaming completions, what's Redwood's recommended retry model? we can't double-apply tokens to downstream side-effects.
[00:03:02] Maya: good question. by default streaming responses are considered non-idempotent; we recommend app-level dedup or at-most-once semantics. for server retries we do token-level retries only for transient infra errors and we avoid resending tokens after flush if the response already started streaming. in short: conservative retries, exponential backoff, and for streaming we surface partials and let the app reconcile.

[00:03:35] Sara: in our case we want a best-effort retry for short-lived infra failures, but if the connection is broken mid-stream we want to avoid duplicating actions.
[00:03:46] Ethan: so operationally we suggest two policies: (A) for idempotent calls (embeddings, stateless completions with no side effects) enable automatic retries up to 3 attempts with jitter; (B) for streaming/side-effecting flows, return an error and let the client decide. also tune timeouts: soft token-level timeout lower than hard connection timeout.

[00:04:15] Tom: that makes sense. back to OOMs - any quick mitigations we can put in place while we root cause?
[00:04:24] Lena: immediate mitigations: reduce batch size, enforce max sequence length cutoff, enable prefix dedupe, and disable the most memory-expensive quant path (if int8 path is causing fragmentation revert to fp16 or a different quant backend). Also consider increasing shared memory pool if you're on managed infra.
[00:04:47] Carlos: reducing batch has a cost impact, that's a bummer for us. but we can try temporary cut to 64 concurrency.

[00:04:56] Ethan: also check for GPU allocator fragmentation: if you have repeated allocate/free patterns at varied sizes, the allocator can fragment and OOM even though free total would be enough. nvml/cuda-mem-report around the time of OOM helps. we'll provide instrumentation commands.

[00:05:20] Tom: can you explain the kv cache eviction strategy? we've noticed stale entries piling up.
[00:05:27] Ethan: by default it's LRU with a global budget per-GPU; but when using dedicated pools we can tune per-request budget or enable a proactive eviction for requests over X tokens. if you have largely disjoint requests, cache hit rate will be low and the cache becomes memory overhead.
[00:05:46] Sara: is there an option to checkpoint kv to host memory to reduce GPU residency?
[00:05:52] Lena: yes there's an experimental host-backed KV option - it swaps cold KV pages to host pinned memory, which reduces GPU usage but adds a latency tail. for your streaming SLAs it might be acceptable for cold prefixes. we can enable that for the repro run.
[00:06:12] Maya: quick aside on quantization: int8 kernels can increase temporary workspace due to packing and additional buffers; some backends allocate extra scratch space per attention block - that can push you over limit. also model compilation choices (tensor core use) can alter peak. we should compare the nvprof traces.

[00:06:36] Tom: ok, we can run fp16 vs int8 traces. what about driver versions - could that cause context timeouts?
[00:06:43] Jon: yes, certain driver+cuda combos have bugs where long-running kernels trigger watchdog. also if the node is running display drivers or TDR is enabled in OS, that causes timeouts. best practice: use server-mode drivers and disable watchdog for GPU compute nodes. we'll verify your driver stack.

[00:07:05] Carlos: we do use a mixed cluster, some dev nodes have display drivers; we might be hitting that.

[00:07:12] Ethan: another angle: preemption/reclaim on cloud instances. if you're on preemptible GPUs, OOM or context loss can be from host reclaim. check cloud events.

[00:07:26] Tom: we're on a mix - some dedicated committed capacity, some spot. nightly jobs run on spot and that's when most failures spike.

[00:07:35] Maya: ok that explains intermittent nature. action: run repro on dedicated non-preemptible node to see if failure reproduces. if it does, it's allocator/kv/quant; if not, preemption.

[00:07:48] Sara: about timeouts, our client sees 'stream read timeout' after ~30s of silence then retries, which sometimes collides with server-side retry and causes duplicate completions.
[00:08:00] Ethan: set keepalive heartbeats from server during long-gen to avoid client timeout; also recommend client retry with idempotency token. for streaming, send small chunk heartbeats every few seconds so proxies don't cut idle connections.

[00:08:18] Tom: good point, we have idle detection in our LB at 30s.

[00:08:25] Lena: We'll add guidance: set LB idle timeout > expected max chunk interval or use application-level pings. also on Redwood side we support chunk-level heartbeats in streaming protocol.

[00:08:40] Priya: on the retrial semantics, what does Redwood do for partial response visibility in logs? we need to correlate partials to trace IDs.
[00:08:49] Jon: we attach request_id and sequence_token to log lines; partials are emitted with the same request_id and monotonic token index. we'll share the log schema.

[00:09:00] Tom: about debugging: what specific logs do you need from our side?
[00:09:06] Ethan: nvml GPU memory snapshots at 1s cadence around failure, dmesg, driver logs, the runtime debug trace (we'll provide a debug-enabled binary to run for repro), and a minimal request that reproduces. also memory allocator stack traces if possible (jemalloc/allocator hooks).

[00:09:22] Sara: ok we'll collect those.

[00:09:28] Maya: let's walk through a proposed repro plan: (1) reproduce deterministically on dedicated node with same model and batch size, (2) run with fp16 baseline, (3) run with int8 quant path, (4) capture nvprof and nvml, (5) if OOM persists, run with host-backed KV to see memory reduction, (6) test reduced batch size and measure p50/p95 latency impact.

[00:10:02] Tom: timeline?
[00:10:05] Maya: we can turn around initial repro instrumentation in 2-3 business days once you give traces.

[00:10:12] Priya: any permanent mitigations you recommend? we want to avoid constant manual tuning.

[00:10:18] Ethan: long-term: (a) implement adaptive batching tied to p95 latency and memory pressure signals, (b) dynamic KV eviction thresholds based on sequence length histograms, (c) preferring dedupe-friendly prompt templates, (d) lockstep driver and CUDA versions validated in our compatibility matrix, and (e) conservative retry/timeouts for streaming.

[00:10:42] Carlos: adaptive batching sounds interesting but complex. does Redwood expose metrics we can feed into autoscaler?

[00:10:49] Lena: yes exporter metrics include per-GPU memory headroom, kv cache resident, and batch queue length. you can hook these into K8s/HPA or our autoscaling policies for Dedicated.

[00:11:02] Sara: will you share recommended autoscale thresholds?

[00:11:05] Maya: yes - default safe thresholds: maintain >10% GPU free memory, cap concurrent streams per-GPU at N (we'll calculate based on model size), and tiered fallback to smaller model or dedicated larger GPU if falling below threshold. we'll include numbers in the follow-up.

[00:11:21] Tom: any notes on VPC/on-prem differences? we're evaluating Private for full control.

[00:11:27] Ethan: on-prem you control drivers and watchdog, so less surprise from display drivers. but you also need to ensure good kernel/NUMA layout, pinned memory config, and PCIe peer settings. in VPC we can automate most of that but need host permissions for certain debug ops.

[00:11:46] Priya: good - we may push to Private for stability if repro is non-cloud issue.

[00:11:53] Maya: ok let's capture explicit next steps (we'll do these now):
[00:11:57] - Aegis to export request traces, p95 seq histograms, and indicate which runs were spot vs dedicated (Sara/Tom)
[00:12:05] - Redwood (Ethan) to provide debug run instructions, debug binary, and a small checklist for nvml/dmesg collection
[00:12:12] - Run repro on non-preemptible dedicated node and report results (Tom/Ethan)
[00:12:18] - Follow-up call next week to review traces and plan pilot adjustments (Maya)

[00:12:28] Tom: one last question - for the streaming retry policy, will Redwood expose a header to indicate partial completion so our downstreams can dedupe?
[00:12:36] Jon: yes we can emit a completion-status header with request_id and final_token_index; we'll add that to the schema we share.

[00:12:45] Sara: good, that'll help.

[00:12:48] Maya: cool. anything else from Aegis?
[00:12:51] Priya: no, thanks. Appreciate the thoroughness.

[00:12:55] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll kick off the action items. I'll share the debug doc and schedule the follow-up.

[00:58:00] <<meeting ended>>

Notes on transcript quality: some vendor names may be slightly mis-transcribed in the live capture (e.g., 'K V cash' instead of KV cache). occasional filler words and overlaps remain.

References/shared artifacts: "redwood-debug-runbook.md" (Redwood will share), nvml collection commands, example request trace snippet (Aegis to provide).

End of transcript.
